I'm 83 this year, and I've been farming these flat fields in Quzhou since I was a boy. My son works in Handan and comes back to help with the machine hiring, but I still decide what goes into the ground. I've got 5 mu of land, and I'm not changing what has fed us for sixty years: winter wheat and then summer corn. The wheat went in last October — I use improved seed from the village supply shop, the same kind my neighbor Old Wang buys, not those expensive new things. Before sowing I put down compound fertilizer and then topdress with urea when the wheat greens up in spring. I figure about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu total — I heard the county extension people say we should use less, but my neighbor tried cutting back two years ago and his yield dropped, so I'd rather spend a bit more than risk an empty stomach. I put down about 6 kg each of phosphorus and potassium too. The wheat needs three irrigations: one when it wakes up, one at jointing, and one when the grain is filling. Water from the tube well costs money, but you can't skip it in Quzhou. I spray twice — herbicide early, and once more if I see bugs. Last fall I prepared the ground with the rotary tiller, same as always. If spring doesn't turn too dry, I expect around 420 kg per mu.

After we harvest the wheat in early June, the window is tight. I hire the machine to plant hybrid corn straight into the wheat stubble — no time to plough again, and at my age I can't handle turning soil anyway. I put down a bit less for the corn than the wheat, about 13 kg nitrogen per mu, and 5 kg each of phosphorus and potassium. Summer usually brings rain, so I'll irrigate once unless July turns very dry. Two pesticide sprays: herbicide right after planting, and insecticide if the worms show up. If the weather is normal, the corn should give me 500 kg per mu. I'm not trying anything new. New things are risks for young people with money to lose. I know this system; it gives us flour and a little cash. That is enough.
